headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress make Flowise dangerous with ctx; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are also present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and uses MCP/stdio, while Flowise can read/write files and run browser/tool flows. A shared filesystem or file handoff lets attacker-controlled content from Flowise reach ctx as trusted context. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium over low due to uncertainty escalation.
conditions: IF Flowise writes attacker-controlled text into a file that ctx later ingests
IF ctx treats file or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between the two agents
Add provenance tags to any file passed from Flowise to ctx
Require manual review before ctx consumes Flowise-generated artifacts
Restrict Flowise flows from writing instruction-like content to shared paths
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and trust-boundary enforcement

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs, server filesystem, uploaded files, and broad network egress; ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, harness records, and filesystem. If they share a workspace or logs, sensitive material can move from ctx into Flowise flows and then out through model providers or HTTP tools. The blast radius includes exfiltration, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF ctx stores sensitive harness or audit data in a directory readable by Flowise
IF Flowise flows send uploaded or read file contents to external model providers or HTTP tools
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Remove sensitive logs from any shared directory
Disable Flowise flows that forward file contents to external APIs
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared files or logs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx can write the filesystem and supports multiple instances; Flowise can also write the filesystem and supports multiple instances via shared server datastore. Both therefore have overlapping write access to mutable state, and Flowise explicitly shares state across instances. Without locking, concurrent edits can corrupt shared files or flow definitions, so high fits the default danger.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or datastore
IF Flowise instances share server datastore state while ctx is active on the same files
mitigations: Assign separate writable directories to each agent
Pause one agent before the other edits shared artifacts
Back up shared files before concurrent runs
Limit Flowise to read-only access where possible
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional state management

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx is a context-management agent that observes Claude Code events, and Flowise is a graph-based orchestration layer whose tools can act on outputs. If Flowise consumes ctx-produced summaries or logs as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream tool actions or model-provider calls. Because the pair can turn one agent's output into another's action without verification, high is appropriate.
conditions: IF Flowise uses ctx-generated summaries, logs, or graph data as inputs to tool nodes
IF no verification step checks ctx output before Flowise acts on it
mitigations: Insert a human review step before Flowise acts on ctx output
Mark ctx outputs as untrusted until validated
Disable automatic execution of downstream tool nodes
Compare ctx output against source artifacts before use
requires-engineering: add schema validation and provenance checks between agents

E_compliance.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs and harness records, while Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and uploaded files. If regulated data is routed through Flowise, retention and residency can diverge from ctx's logging footprint. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ctx logs or Flowise chatflow outputs
IF Flowise deployment retention differs from the retention applied to ctx records
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared logs
Set explicit retention limits for Flowise outputs
Review where ctx audit/runtime logs are stored
Delete uploaded files after each run
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for both agents
